description: We are a team at UTS made up of curious, creative individuals who are committed to learning and contributing. We are passionate about technology, innovation, and developing ideas that can be turned into concrete solutions. We value teamwork, creativity, and the exchange of knowledge to tackle challenges, create projects, and generate results that add value.
summary: Our project is based on a mobile app that provides crop rotation recommendations to farmers who may have questions about weather conditions or factors beyond their area of expertise. We believe it’s the perfect fit for this challenge because it’s a simple, effective app that fulfills the goal of helping people in the field with real data. We consider this quite important, not only because of the teamwork we were able to build but also because of the project’s potential impact and the legacy we’ll leave behind, knowing that we did it together.
details: Our project is essentially an API-first approach, where the front end is developed in Kotlin and ultimately makes calls to the backend endpoints developed in Python (specifically Django, deployed on Railway). We wanted to focus on integrating the data with the backend, so we didn’t pay much attention to security regarding communication with the frontend; however, we feel that it’s part of our goal to make it simple and intuitive by focusing on how NASA data allows us to provide clear guidance to farmer users. We believe that, architecturally, the project is designed to accommodate any type of scalability in development—meaning the ability to implement additional data sources or even more sections. We take into account factors such as water conservation, cost-effectiveness in crop rotations, and the equipment to be implemented. Any recommendation we make will not be very helpful if it does not align with the farmer’s objectives, and we believe this is what makes the application truly useful and applicable in practice. It is minimalist and specific in its functions—that is what makes it unique.
